claims.text: The initial material is a powder-metallurgy NbTiVZr-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
A thin Ag interlayer can be incorporated into the NbTiVZr-based alloy by transient liquid phase sintering.
Optimizing Ag content and interlayer thickness will produce a continuous, interconnected Ag network.
Ag is molten during sintering at 1100–1200 °C.
Molten Ag preferentially wets the NbTiVZr-based HEA particles.
Cooling after sintering causes Ag to resolidify as finely tuned films or shells at particle boundaries.
The boundary Ag films or shells form an interconnected network within the HEA matrix.
The interconnected Ag network acts as conductive bridges that enhance electron and phonon heat transport.
Controlled Ag incorporation avoids deleterious weak interfaces.
The primary refractory HEA matrix remains the load-bearing phase after Ag incorporation.
Refractory alloys generally provide strength and stability at elevated temperatures.
Powder-metallurgy processing can provide ductility advantages over arc melting or mechanically activated SPS processing in refractory alloys.
The Ag-modified intermediate layer will exhibit up to approximately 30% higher effective thermal conductivity than the Ag-free HEA baseline.
The Ag-modified layer will retain tensile and fatigue performance comparable to the current standard HEA intermediate layer.
The proposed thermal and mechanical benefits will persist at 600–750 °C under high thermal flux and mechanical loading.
Improper Ag content or interlayer thickness could produce weak interfaces.
Improper Ag incorporation could lead to brittle intermetallic phases.
The hypothesis can be tested against an otherwise comparable Ag-free NbTiVZr-based HEA control while varying Ag content and interlayer thickness.

contradictions.description: The predicted gain is stated as 'up to approximately 30%,' but the falsification rule requires an improvement of approximately 30% or more. An outcome below 30% could be compatible with an 'up to 30%' prediction yet would be declared falsifying.
